title: An API for a Notes App
prompt: A notes app runs on phones and the web. Users create, edit and delete notes, and scroll through their notes newest first; some users have thousands. Phone users often keep an old version of the app for months. Design the API.
facts: 1 million users, each making about 20 requests a day
Peak traffic is about 5 times the average
Some users have more than 5,000 notes
Phones lose their connection often, so requests are retried
scope: Sharing notes and sign-in are out of scope

requirements: Lists the operations: list, create, read, edit, delete
States that old app versions must keep working and that retries must not damage data
estimation: Average load: 10⁶ × 20 = 2 × 10⁷ requests a day ÷ 10⁵ ≈ 200 per second; peak about 1,000 per second
design: REST resources such as GET /notes?limit=20&after=<cursor>, POST /notes, GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE /notes/{id}
Correct status codes for success and for common errors (201 on create, 404 for a missing note, 400 for invalid input, 403 for someone else's note)
data: Cursor pagination over an index on (user_id, updated_at, id) or similar, so deep pages stay fast and new notes do not shift pages
Versioning: add optional fields freely; breaking changes go to a new version such as /v2/
tradeoffs: Explains which requests are safe to retry: PUT and DELETE are idempotent, a retried POST can create a duplicate note (an idempotency key fixes it, SD 7)
Or another trade-off with its condition, such as keeping /v1 running costs work while old apps remain

fullMarkDesigns: REST API under /v1 with cursor pagination ordered by update time then id, PUT to replace a note's text, and DELETE. About 200 requests per second on average, 1,000 at peak. Retries: PUT and DELETE are safe; POST may duplicate, so the app sends an idempotency key. New fields are optional; breaking changes would go to /v2.

Same resources, but edits use PATCH for the title or text and creation uses PUT /notes/{client-generated-id}, which makes creation idempotent and safe to retry. Pagination by cursor; status codes as usual. Trade-off: the server must check that client-made ids are unique.

assumptions: Notes are private to one user
reference.design:
Resources: GET /v1/notes?limit=20&after=<cursor> lists notes newest first; POST /v1/notes creates (201 with the new note's address); GET, PUT and DELETE /v1/notes/{id} read, replace and remove one note. A missing note returns 404, another user's note 403, invalid input 400.
Paging uses a cursor of the last note's update time and id, over an index on (user_id, updated_at, id), so a user with 5,000 notes scrolls as fast at the end as at the start.
Load: 10⁶ × 20 ÷ 10⁵ ≈ 200 requests per second, about 1,000 at peak.
Retries: PUT and DELETE can be sent again safely; a retried POST could create a second note, so the app sends an idempotency key with it. New optional fields keep /v1 working for old apps.
alternatives: Offset pagination: simpler, but slow for deep pages and repeats notes when new ones arrive
gRPC: possible between services, but REST with JSON is simpler for phones and the web

title: Live Scores for Sports Day
prompt: A school holds a sports day, and parents follow the scores live on their phones. Design how the scores reach the phones.
facts: About 3,000 parents keep the score page open for 4 hours
Scores change about 120 times during the day
A new score must appear on phones within 5 seconds
One server handles about 250 requests per second, or about 5,000 open connections
Parents only watch; they do not send anything
scope: Entering scores is out of scope

requirements: States the 5-second update requirement and that data flows only from server to phones
estimation: Polling every 5 s: 3,000 ÷ 5 = 600 requests per second, more than 2 servers at their limit
Server push: 3,000 open connections and 120 × 3,000 = 360,000 messages over 4 hours = 14,400 s, about 25 per second
design: A delivery method chosen with a reason: server-sent events, WebSocket, long polling, or polling with enough servers
The path from the score store to the phones
data: Where the current scores live (one small table or a cache) and how many servers the chosen method needs from the estimate
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: phones lose signal, so they must reconnect and fetch the current scores; or polling wastes most requests because scores change about once every 2 minutes

fullMarkDesigns: Server-sent events: each phone opens one connection; the server pushes a message when a score changes, about 25 messages per second. 3,000 connections fit on one server (limit about 5,000). On reconnect, the phone first fetches the current scores. Trade-off: one server is a single point of failure for the day.

Polling every 4 s with a cached score page: 3,000 ÷ 4 = 750 requests per second, so 4 servers behind a load balancer at 75% of their limit, or more for headroom. Simple and works on any network. Trade-off: almost every poll returns no change (about 120 changes against 3,600 polls per phone), which costs servers but is affordable here.

assumptions: Scores change about once every 2 minutes on average
Parents are on mobile networks that drop sometimes
reference.design:
Phones open the score page and then keep one server-sent events connection. When a score is entered, the server sends it to every open connection.
Load: 3,000 open connections, under one server's 5,000; 120 changes × 3,000 phones = 360,000 messages over 14,400 seconds, about 25 per second.
Polling every 5 seconds instead would cost 3,000 ÷ 5 = 600 requests per second, more than two servers at their limit, while almost every answer says "no change".
When a phone reconnects after losing signal, it first loads the current scores, then listens again.
alternatives: WebSocket: works, but parents never send anything, so two-way messaging is unused
Polling with enough servers: simpler and fine at this size, at the cost of many empty answers
